NAC.about: Precursor of glutathione, the main cell antioxidant: fewer exacerbations of COPD, liver protection.
NAC.caution: N-acetylcysteine is a precursor of glutathione. 4 Cochrane reviews in the database! For COPD: reduces the frequency of exacerbations. For acute liver failure (non-paracetamol): Cochrane. For H. pylori (adjuvant): Cochrane. For sepsis: Cochrane. For psychiatry (OCD, trichotillomania, bipolar): there is RCT with positive data. Dose: 600-1200 mg 2 times/day. Safe, side effects: GI.
NAC.food_sources: There is no separate food source: NAC is a cysteine derivative; cysteine ​​is found in meat, eggs, and oatmeal.
NAC.guidelines: Cochrane: in COPD there are fewer exacerbations (RR 0.87) at doses up to 600 mg; there is no benefit for sepsis; for H. pylori - adjunct.
NAC.how_to_choose: Any L-form NAC, 600–1200 mg/day. Expensive “sports” versions are not needed - reviews are based on the classic form.

interactions.note: enhances the effect, risk of hypotension

mechs: Mucolytic and antioxidant effect: thinning mucus in the respiratory tract
Fewer exacerbations of COPD at 600 mg/day and below
Antimicrobial adjuvant: destruction of H. pylori biofilms, bactericidal activity
Higher eradication of H. pylori in combination with antibiotics
Glutathione precursor: neutralize toxic metabolites in the liver
Less risk of transplantation in paracetamol liver failure
NAC.myths: “Antioxidant = health” – did not reduce mortality in sepsis (Cochrane). “Higher dose is better” - for COPD >600 mg without benefit; works up to 600 mg.
NAC.name: NAC
NAC.onset: There is no immediate effect: with COPD, exacerbations are less frequent over a distance, NAC is taken in courses.
NAC.title: NAC
NAC.upper_limit: No formal UL listed - no toxicity data available.
NAC.who_needs: For COPD with frequent exacerbations; liver failure (including paracetamol); resistant H. pylori.
